analysis.one_liner: Sets mandatory federal stability testing and warning standards for dressers to prevent tip-over deaths of young children.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the dresser-safety bill without a single opposing vote in September 2022, but the House never brought it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Dressers and other tall clothing furniture can tip over when children climb on them, sometimes fatally. This bill orders the Consumer Product Safety Commission to replace the current voluntary industry standard with a mandatory federal rule, including repeatable tests that simulate real-world use — a child's weight, carpeted floors, loaded drawers, several drawers open at once — plus warning labels. It passed the Senate unanimously but the House of Representatives never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children, who get a federally enforceable guarantee that every dresser and chest sold in the U.S. has passed tests simulating real tip-over conditions, rather than relying on the furniture industry's voluntary standard.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission to issue a final mandatory safety standard for freestanding clothing storage units within one year, protecting children from tip-over-related death or injury [S2] [S5].

Mandates objective, repeatable tests that simulate real-world conditions: children up to 60 pounds, placement on carpet, loaded and multiple open drawers, and dynamic force — not just a static test [S5].
Covers all clothing storage units 27 inches and taller and requires tip-over warning requirements, which the Commission may strengthen beyond the industry's ASTM F2057-19 standard [S5].
The Commission must consult consumer groups, manufacturers, craft furniture makers, and independent child product engineers when assessing whether the voluntary standard is adequate [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Furniture manufacturers, importers, and retailers bear the cost of testing every unit and adding warnings; some of that cost likely shows up in furniture prices. Small craft and handmade furniture makers face the same testing regime as large producers.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory testing and warning-label requirements impose real compliance costs on manufacturers, including small craft and handmade furniture shops, and those costs are likely passed to consumers in furniture prices [S5].

The bill gives the industry's own voluntary standard a fast track to become federal law if it meets the requirements, so furniture makers would largely write the technical details they must then meet [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — preventing tip-over deaths and injuries of small children — is concentrated and grave; the cost is a compliance expense spread across the furniture market. The bill's main design weakness is the fast-track adoption of the industry-drafted voluntary standard, though the Commission retains authority to reject or strengthen it.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it without opposition in September 2022, but the House simply held it at the desk — never scheduled a vote — and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator Casey in November 2021 and referred to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee [S1] [S7].
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably in May 2022 and formally reported it with an amendment in September 2022 [S7].
On September 29, 2022, the Senate passed the bill by unanimous consent — no roll-call vote and no senator opposed [S7].
The House received the bill on September 30, 2022, and held it at the desk; no committee referral, no floor vote, and no further action through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Furniture manufacturers avoided the mandatory testing and warning costs the bill would have imposed, and no family got the federal tip-over standard it promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Furniture makers; no new mandatory safety costs

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through the Senate Commerce Committee to unanimous passage.

for.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of committee favorably with an amendment in September 2022, placing it on the Senate calendar for consideration.

for.name: 12 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan backing before Senate passage.

against.name: House leadership of the 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill from the Senate on September 30, 2022 and left it 'held at the desk' — never scheduled committee consideration or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan cosponsorship (12 Senate Democrats and 1 Republican) and passed the Senate by unanimous consent, so no party opposed it; the obstacle was House inaction, not a party split.

industries.note: The bill would impose mandatory tip-over testing and warning-label costs on every clothing storage unit sold, and its fast-track path lets an industry-drafted voluntary standard become the federal rule. The public benefit — fewer child tip-over deaths — is exactly what the industry avoided when the bill died in the House.
